To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of others in an experiment, when the others have the power to reward the subject, increases the speed with which subjects respond, while when they have the power to punish, subjects respond with more objectionable responses.

(1) the mere presence drive model does not explain the effects of social observation on word association responding; (2) the self-presentation model does explain the effects of observation on word association, and (3) the self-preservation model, when revised to include information-processing considerations, also explains the effects of incentive on word association

Observation, but not Incentration, resulted in a lower frequency of objectionable responses, but not in a higher frequency of common responses, and in a higher speed of responses, while Incentration, but not Observation resulted in a higher frequency and speed of common responses.

the results of the experiment are best explained by the information-processing version of the self-presentation model of social presence.

social presence effects in a word association task are not adequately accounted for by a mere presence drive explanation, but are more adequately accounted for by an information-processing self-presentation explanation.

social presence effects are due to self-presentation.
